This banking institution received a concession to print its own banknotes in this particular country where the store was located during the 20th century.  Based on the given details, in what year was this store founded?

**Vientiane**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-5) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and largest city of [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"). Comprising the 5 [urban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area")[districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Laos "Districts of Laos") of [Vientiane Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Prefecture "Vientiane Prefecture"), the city is located on the banks of the [Mekong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mekong "Mekong"), close to the border with [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"). Vientiane was the administrative capital during [French rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_protectorate_of_Laos "French protectorate of Laos"). The city had a population of 840,000 as of the 2023 census. [Pha That Luang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pha_That_Luang "Pha That Luang"), an icon of Buddhism, is located in Vientiane. Other Buddhist temples can be found there, such as [Haw Phra Kaew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haw_Phra_Kaew "Haw Phra Kaew"), which formerly housed the [Emerald Buddha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha "Emerald Buddha").

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

"Vientiane" is the French spelling derived from the Lao _Viangchan_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-:0-4) The name was previously written "ວຽງຈັນທນ໌" and later sometimes written "ວຽງຈັນ". In Lao, _viang_ (ວຽງ) refers to a 'walled city' with ຈັນ _chan_ of two [homonyms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homonym "Homonym"):[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-6)

*   one shortened from ຈັນທນ໌ deriving from [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_language "Sanskrit language"): चन्दन _candana_ (pronounced[[t͡ɕand̪ana]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Sanskrit "Help:IPA/Sanskrit")) '[sandalwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandalwood "Sandalwood")' thus translated as the 'walled city of sandalwood'
*   another meant 'moon' previously distinguished in writing as "ຈັນທຣ໌" (from Skt. चन्द्र _[chandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra "Chandra")_), thus referring to the 'walled city of the moon'.

Other romanisations include "Viangchan" and "Wiangchan".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Ban-talat-Mon-inscription.jpg/250px-Ban-talat-Mon-inscription.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ban-talat-Mon-inscription.jpg)

Ban Tha Lat, [Mon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon_language "Mon language") inscription (9th CE), was found in 1968, in an area where other pieces of archaeological evidence testified to a Mon presence. It was exhibited at [Ho Phra Keo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haw_Phra_Kaew "Haw Phra Kaew") Museum, Vientiane, Laos[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-9)

### Dvaravati city state kingdoms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Dvaravati city state kingdoms")]

By the 6th century in the [Chao Phraya River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_Phraya_River "Chao Phraya River") Valley, [Mon peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon_people "Mon people") had coalesced to create the [Dvaravati kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvaravati "Dvaravati"). In the north, [Haripunjaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haripunjaya "Haripunjaya") ([Lamphun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamphun "Lamphun")) emerged as a rival power to the [Dvaravati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvaravati "Dvaravati"). By the 8th century the Mon had pushed north to create city states, in Fa Daet (what later is [Kalasin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalasin "Kalasin"), northeastern Thailand), Sri Gotapura (Sikhottabong) near [Tha Khek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tha_Khek_District "Tha Khek District"), Laos, [Muang Sua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muang_Sua "Muang Sua") ([Luang Prabang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang "Luang Prabang")), and Chantaburi (Vientiane). In the 8th century CE, Sri Gotapura (Sikhottabong) was the “strongest of these early city states”, and controlled trade throughout the middle Mekong region. The city states were “loosely bound politically, but were culturally similar” and introduced [Therevada Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therevada_Buddhism "Therevada Buddhism") from [Sri Lankan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka") missionaries throughout the region.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Viravond-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Manich-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-13):6,7[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-15)

### Transition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transition")]

A reference to the name Vientiane can be seen on a Vietnamese inscription of Duke [Đỗ Anh Vũ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%90%E1%BB%97_Anh_V%C5%A9 "Đỗ Anh Vũ"), dated 1159 during the Khmer-Viet conflict. The inscription says that in 1135, Văn Đan (Vientiane), a vassal of Zhenla ([Khmer Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Empire "Khmer Empire")), invaded [Nghe An](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nghe_An "Nghe An"), and was repelled by the Duke; the Duke led an army chased the invaders as far as Vũ Ôn? (unattested), and then returned with captives.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Taylor1995-16):65

Decades later, Phraya Chanthaburi (lit.'King of Chanthaburi'; Vientiane), together with his elder brother Tao Gwa of Mueang Kaew Prakan—a polity sometimes identified with [Xiangkhouang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiangkhouang "Xiangkhouang") ([Muang Phuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muang_Phuan "Muang Phuan"))[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-chian-17)—launched a military invasion of the [Ngoenyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoenyang "Ngoenyang") Kingdom of the [Tai Yuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Yuan "Tai Yuan") in 1171 CE. The invasion failed as the [Ngoenyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoenyang "Ngoenyang") ruler Khun Chin sought military assistance from his nephews, the Chueang brothers. After successfully expelling the invaders, the younger [Chueang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chueang "Chueang") marched eastward, annexed polities, and eventually captured [Muang Phuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muang_Phuan "Muang Phuan").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-cm-18):9[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-chiang-19):76–9 He then appointed his middle son, also named Chueang, as ruler of Muang Phuan, and his youngest son, Lao Pao, as ruler of Vientiane.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-chiang-19):82–3

### Lan Xang, and French colony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lan Xang, and French colony")]

In 1354, when [Fa Ngum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fa_Ngum "Fa Ngum") founded the kingdom of [Lan Xang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lan_Xang "Lan Xang"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Coedes-20):223 Vientiane became an administrative city. King [Setthathirath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setthathirath "Setthathirath") officially established it as the capital of Lan Xang in 1563, to avoid Burmese invasion.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-21)

During French rule, the Vietnamese were encouraged to migrate to Laos, which resulted in 53% of the population of Vientiane being Vietnamese in the year 1943.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-MartinStuart-FoxA-22) As late as 1945, the French drew up a plan to move Vietnamese population to 3 areas (i.e. the Vientiane Plain, the [Savannakhet region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannakhet_Province "Savannakhet Province"), and the [Bolaven Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolaven_Plateau "Bolaven Plateau")), which was interrupted by the Japanese invasion of Indochina.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-MartinStuart-FoxA-22) If this plan had been implemented, according to [Martin Stuart-Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Stuart-Fox "Martin Stuart-Fox"), the Lao might well have lost control over their own country.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-MartinStuart-FoxA-22)

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Vientiane fell and was occupied by Japanese forces.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated4-23) On 9 March 1946, French paratroopers arrived and reoccupied the city on 24 April 1946.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated1-24):736

### Independence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independence")]

After the [Laotian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laotian_Civil_War "Laotian Civil War") broke out between the [Royal Lao Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Lao_Government "Royal Lao Government") and the [Pathet Lao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathet_Lao "Pathet Lao"), in August 1960, [Kong Le](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Le "Kong Le") seized the capital Vientiane and insisted that [Souvanna Phouma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souvanna_Phouma "Souvanna Phouma") become prime minister. In December, [Phoumi Nosavan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoumi_Nosavan "Phoumi Nosavan") then seized the capital, overthrew the Phouma Government, and installed [Boun Oum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boun_Oum "Boun Oum") as prime minister. In 1975, Pathet Lao troops moved towards the city and Americans began evacuating the capital. On 23 August 1975, a contingent of 50 Pathet Lao women symbolically liberated the city. On December 2, 1975, the Laotian Civil War was officially declared over, when the monarchy was forced into exile.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated1-24)

## Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Tourism")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Buddha_park%2C_lao_pdr.jpg/250px-Buddha_park%2C_lao_pdr.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buddha_park,_lao_pdr.jpg)

[Buddha Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddha_Park "Buddha Park")

The capital attracts tourists to its temples and Buddhist monuments. An attraction is [Pha That Luang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pha_That_Luang "Pha That Luang"), a national cultural monument of Laos and 1 of its [stupas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stupa "Stupa"). It was originally built in 1566 by King [Setthathirath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setthathirath "Setthathirath") and was restored in 1953. The golden stupa is 45 metres (148 ft) tall and is believed to contain a relic of the Buddha.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated2-31)

The [Wat Si Muang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Si_Muang "Wat Si Muang") temple was built on the ruins of a Khmer Hindu shrine, the remains of which can be seen behind the [ordination hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordination_hall "Ordination hall").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated3-32) It was built in 1563 and is believed to be guarded by the spirit of a local girl, Nang Si. Legend tells that Nang Si, who was pregnant at the time, leapt to her death as a sacrifice, just as the pillar was being lowered into the hole. In front of the temple stands a statue of King [Sisavang Vong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisavang_Vong "Sisavang Vong").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated3-32)

The memorial monument, [Patuxai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patuxai "Patuxai"), built between 1957 and 1968, is a landmark in the city.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated2-31)

[Buddha Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddha_Park "Buddha Park") was built in 1958 by [Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Pu_Bunleua_Sulilat "Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat") and contains a collection of Buddhist and Hindu sculptures, scattered amongst gardens and trees. The park is 28 kilometres (17 mi) south of Vientiane at the edge of the [Mekong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mekong_River "Mekong River").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-33)

Other sites include:

*   [Haw Phra Kaew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haw_Phra_Kaew "Haw Phra Kaew"), former temple, later a museum and shops
*   [Lao National Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_National_Museum "Lao National Museum")
*   [Kaysone Phomvihane Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaysone_Phomvihane_Museum "Kaysone Phomvihane Museum")
*   [Talat Sao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talat_Sao "Talat Sao"), a morning market
*   [That Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That_Dam "That Dam"), a stupa
*   [Wat Ong Teu Mahawihan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Ong_Teu_Mahawihan "Wat Ong Teu Mahawihan"), a Buddhist monastery
*   [Wat Sri Chomphu Ong Tue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Sri_Chomphu_Ong_Tue "Wat Sri Chomphu Ong Tue"), a Buddhist temple
*   [Wat Si Saket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Si_Saket "Wat Si Saket"), a Buddhist temple
*   Wat Sok Pa Luang, a Buddhist temple
*   [Settha Palace Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settha_Palace_Hotel "Settha Palace Hotel"), established 1932
*   The Sanjiang Market[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-34)
*   [Kualao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kualao_Restaurant "Kualao Restaurant"), a restaurant

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Culture")]

### Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Media")]

Vientiane is the centre of Laos' national media. It hosts the headquarters of[Lao National Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_National_Television "Lao National Television")and[Lao National Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_National_Radio "Lao National Radio"). The city is also served by the municipal broadcaster[VTE9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VTE9?action=edit&redlink=1 "VTE9 (page does not exist)"), as well as[CRI Vientiane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRI_Vientiane "CRI Vientiane"), a station affiliated with [China Radio International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Radio_International "China Radio International").

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Education")]

The [National University of Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_University_of_Laos "National University of Laos") is in Vientiane.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-35)

International schools include:

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

Vientiane has experienced economic growth from foreign investment.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-37) In 2011, the [stock exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_Securities_Exchange "Lao Securities Exchange") opened with two listed company stocks, with the cooperation of [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-38) At the end of 2025, the Laos government announced that the economy of the city had grown by an average of 5.34% per year over the last five years, and that industrial and agricultural shares of the economy declined while the service economy gained in its share of the market.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-39) As of 2026, the economy continues to grow from aforementioned foreign investment, including the private health sector and the [electric vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle "Electric vehicle") sector.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-40) At the beginning of 2026, the Lao government announced an initiative to accrue roughly US$30,000,000 in sought investments[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] to drive the city's economic growth.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-41)

### Bus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Bus")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Vientiane_Bus_-_BRT.jpg/250px-Vientiane_Bus_-_BRT.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vientiane_Bus_-_BRT.jpg)

Vientiane eBRT Bus

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Meter_Taxi_in_Vientiane_01.jpg/250px-Meter_Taxi_in_Vientiane_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meter_Taxi_in_Vientiane_01.jpg)

Older taxis in Vientiane are being replaced by newer Chinese-made cars, like this [Soueast Lioncel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soueast "Soueast").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-42)

There are regular [bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus "Bus") services connecting [Vientiane Bus Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Bus_Station "Vientiane Bus Station") with the rest of the country. In Vientiane, regular bus services around the city are provided by Vientiane Capital State Bus Enterprise.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-43)

Vientiane constructed its first [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) service in 2024 under the Vientiane Urban Transport Project (VSUTP) of Laos' [Ministry of Public Works and Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Public_Works_and_Transport_(Laos) "Ministry of Public Works and Transport (Laos)").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-44) There will be three BRT lines with a total route length of 13.9 km within the capital area. The construction of the BRT was 90% completed in the end of July 2025 and it was scheduled for free trial operation in August 2025, with a total of 55 buses manufactured in China by Chery Wanda;[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-45) it was then delayed to September 2025.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-46) The BRT service officially opened for free trial from 10 March to 9 May 2026; normal fare operation was due to start on 10 May.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-47)

Shortly after the opening of the BRT free trial, the Laos government planned to expand the BRT to [Wattay International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattay_International_Airport "Wattay International Airport") and [China-Laos Vientiane Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_railway_station "Vientiane railway station") in the future. To mitigate the sudden fuel price surge and fuel shortage caused by the [2026 Middle-East conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Iran_War "2026 Iran War"), it is planned to increase the use of electric vehicles in Laos.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-48)

### Rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Rail")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/2a/Laos-China-Railway_Station_Vientiane.jpg/250px-Laos-China-Railway_Station_Vientiane.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laos-China-Railway_Station_Vientiane.jpg)

Vientiane railway station

A [metre gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_gauge "Metre gauge") railway link over the first bridge was formally inaugurated on 5 March 2009, previously ending at [Thanaleng Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanaleng_Railway_Station "Thanaleng Railway Station"), in Dongphosy village ([Vientiane Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Prefecture "Vientiane Prefecture")), 20 km east of Vientiane.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-guardian-09-50) As of November 2010, Lao officials plan to convert the station into a cargo rail terminal for [freight trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freight_trains "Freight trains"), allowing cargo to be transported from Bangkok into Laos more cheaply than via road.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-trweekly-nov10-51)

The [Boten–Vientiane railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boten%E2%80%93Vientiane_railway "Boten–Vientiane railway") (sometimes referred to as the _China–Laos railway_ or _Laos–China railway_) is a 414 kilometres (257 mi)1,435 mm (4 ft 8+1⁄2 in) [standard gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gauge "Standard gauge") electrified railway in [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"), running between the capital Vientiane and the town of [Boten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boten "Boten") on the border with [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). The line was officially opened on 3 December 2021.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-:6-52) In early 2026 the Lao National Assembly approved the first phase of a 562 km standard-gauge railway which will link Vientiane with the Vung Ang deepwater port on Vietnam's coast, providing landlocked Laos direct access to a major port. The project is part of the government's 2026-2030 National Socio-Economic Development Plan.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-53)

### Air

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Air")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/5b/Wattay_Intl_Airport_Vientiane_Laos.jpg/250px-Wattay_Intl_Airport_Vientiane_Laos.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wattay_Intl_Airport_Vientiane_Laos.jpg)

[Wattay International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattay_International_Airport "Wattay International Airport")

Vientiane is served by [Wattay International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattay_International_Airport "Wattay International Airport") with international connections to other Asian destinations such as [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). [Lao Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_Airlines "Lao Airlines") has regular flights to domestic destinations in the country (including flights daily to [Luang Prabang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang "Luang Prabang"), plus flights weekly to other local destinations).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-54)

## Healthcare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Healthcare")]

Main article: [Health in Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_in_Laos "Health in Laos")

The "Centre Medical de l'Ambassade de France" is available to the foreign community in Laos. The [Mahosot Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahosot_Hospital "Mahosot Hospital") is a local hospital in treating and researching diseases and is connected with the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"). In 2011 the Alliance Clinic opened near the airport, with a connection to Thai hospitals. The Setthathirat International Clinic has foreign doctors. A free, 24/7 ambulance service is provided by [Vientiane Rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Rescue "Vientiane Rescue"), a volunteer-run rescue service established in 2010.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-55)

**Vientiane**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-5) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and largest city of [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"). Comprising the 5 [urban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area")[districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Laos "Districts of Laos") of [Vientiane Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Prefecture "Vientiane Prefecture"), the city is located on the banks of the [Mekong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mekong "Mekong"), close to the border with [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"). Vientiane was the administrative capital during [French rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_protectorate_of_Laos "French protectorate of Laos"). The city had a population of 840,000 as of the 2023 census. [Pha That Luang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pha_That_Luang "Pha That Luang"), an icon of Buddhism, is located in Vientiane. Other Buddhist temples can be found there, such as [Haw Phra Kaew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haw_Phra_Kaew "Haw Phra Kaew"), which formerly housed the [Emerald Buddha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha "Emerald Buddha").

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

"Vientiane" is the French spelling derived from the Lao _Viangchan_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-:0-4) The name was previously written "ວຽງຈັນທນ໌" and later sometimes written "ວຽງຈັນ". In Lao, _viang_ (ວຽງ) refers to a 'walled city' with ຈັນ _chan_ of two [homonyms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homonym "Homonym"):[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-6)

*   one shortened from ຈັນທນ໌ deriving from [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_language "Sanskrit language"): चन्दन _candana_ (pronounced[[t͡ɕand̪ana]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Sanskrit "Help:IPA/Sanskrit")) '[sandalwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandalwood "Sandalwood")' thus translated as the 'walled city of sandalwood'
*   another meant 'moon' previously distinguished in writing as "ຈັນທຣ໌" (from Skt. चन्द्र _[chandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra "Chandra")_), thus referring to the 'walled city of the moon'.

Other romanisations include "Viangchan" and "Wiangchan".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Ban-talat-Mon-inscription.jpg/250px-Ban-talat-Mon-inscription.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ban-talat-Mon-inscription.jpg)

Ban Tha Lat, [Mon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon_language "Mon language") inscription (9th CE), was found in 1968, in an area where other pieces of archaeological evidence testified to a Mon presence. It was exhibited at [Ho Phra Keo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haw_Phra_Kaew "Haw Phra Kaew") Museum, Vientiane, Laos[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-9)

### Dvaravati city state kingdoms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Dvaravati city state kingdoms")]

By the 6th century in the [Chao Phraya River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_Phraya_River "Chao Phraya River") Valley, [Mon peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon_people "Mon people") had coalesced to create the [Dvaravati kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvaravati "Dvaravati"). In the north, [Haripunjaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haripunjaya "Haripunjaya") ([Lamphun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamphun "Lamphun")) emerged as a rival power to the [Dvaravati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvaravati "Dvaravati"). By the 8th century the Mon had pushed north to create city states, in Fa Daet (what later is [Kalasin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalasin "Kalasin"), northeastern Thailand), Sri Gotapura (Sikhottabong) near [Tha Khek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tha_Khek_District "Tha Khek District"), Laos, [Muang Sua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muang_Sua "Muang Sua") ([Luang Prabang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang "Luang Prabang")), and Chantaburi (Vientiane). In the 8th century CE, Sri Gotapura (Sikhottabong) was the “strongest of these early city states”, and controlled trade throughout the middle Mekong region. The city states were “loosely bound politically, but were culturally similar” and introduced [Therevada Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therevada_Buddhism "Therevada Buddhism") from [Sri Lankan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka") missionaries throughout the region.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Viravond-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Manich-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-13):6,7[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-15)

### Transition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transition")]

A reference to the name Vientiane can be seen on a Vietnamese inscription of Duke [Đỗ Anh Vũ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%90%E1%BB%97_Anh_V%C5%A9 "Đỗ Anh Vũ"), dated 1159 during the Khmer-Viet conflict. The inscription says that in 1135, Văn Đan (Vientiane), a vassal of Zhenla ([Khmer Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Empire "Khmer Empire")), invaded [Nghe An](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nghe_An "Nghe An"), and was repelled by the Duke; the Duke led an army chased the invaders as far as Vũ Ôn? (unattested), and then returned with captives.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Taylor1995-16):65

Decades later, Phraya Chanthaburi (lit.'King of Chanthaburi'; Vientiane), together with his elder brother Tao Gwa of Mueang Kaew Prakan—a polity sometimes identified with [Xiangkhouang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiangkhouang "Xiangkhouang") ([Muang Phuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muang_Phuan "Muang Phuan"))[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-chian-17)—launched a military invasion of the [Ngoenyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoenyang "Ngoenyang") Kingdom of the [Tai Yuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Yuan "Tai Yuan") in 1171 CE. The invasion failed as the [Ngoenyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoenyang "Ngoenyang") ruler Khun Chin sought military assistance from his nephews, the Chueang brothers. After successfully expelling the invaders, the younger [Chueang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chueang "Chueang") marched eastward, annexed polities, and eventually captured [Muang Phuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muang_Phuan "Muang Phuan").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-cm-18):9[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-chiang-19):76–9 He then appointed his middle son, also named Chueang, as ruler of Muang Phuan, and his youngest son, Lao Pao, as ruler of Vientiane.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-chiang-19):82–3

### Lan Xang, and French colony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lan Xang, and French colony")]

In 1354, when [Fa Ngum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fa_Ngum "Fa Ngum") founded the kingdom of [Lan Xang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lan_Xang "Lan Xang"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-Coedes-20):223 Vientiane became an administrative city. King [Setthathirath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setthathirath "Setthathirath") officially established it as the capital of Lan Xang in 1563, to avoid Burmese invasion.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-21)

During French rule, the Vietnamese were encouraged to migrate to Laos, which resulted in 53% of the population of Vientiane being Vietnamese in the year 1943.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-MartinStuart-FoxA-22) As late as 1945, the French drew up a plan to move Vietnamese population to 3 areas (i.e. the Vientiane Plain, the [Savannakhet region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannakhet_Province "Savannakhet Province"), and the [Bolaven Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolaven_Plateau "Bolaven Plateau")), which was interrupted by the Japanese invasion of Indochina.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-MartinStuart-FoxA-22) If this plan had been implemented, according to [Martin Stuart-Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Stuart-Fox "Martin Stuart-Fox"), the Lao might well have lost control over their own country.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-MartinStuart-FoxA-22)

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Vientiane fell and was occupied by Japanese forces.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated4-23) On 9 March 1946, French paratroopers arrived and reoccupied the city on 24 April 1946.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated1-24):736

### Independence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Independence")]

After the [Laotian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laotian_Civil_War "Laotian Civil War") broke out between the [Royal Lao Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Lao_Government "Royal Lao Government") and the [Pathet Lao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathet_Lao "Pathet Lao"), in August 1960, [Kong Le](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Le "Kong Le") seized the capital Vientiane and insisted that [Souvanna Phouma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souvanna_Phouma "Souvanna Phouma") become prime minister. In December, [Phoumi Nosavan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoumi_Nosavan "Phoumi Nosavan") then seized the capital, overthrew the Phouma Government, and installed [Boun Oum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boun_Oum "Boun Oum") as prime minister. In 1975, Pathet Lao troops moved towards the city and Americans began evacuating the capital. On 23 August 1975, a contingent of 50 Pathet Lao women symbolically liberated the city. On December 2, 1975, the Laotian Civil War was officially declared over, when the monarchy was forced into exile.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated1-24)

## Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Tourism")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Buddha_park%2C_lao_pdr.jpg/250px-Buddha_park%2C_lao_pdr.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buddha_park,_lao_pdr.jpg)

[Buddha Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddha_Park "Buddha Park")

The capital attracts tourists to its temples and Buddhist monuments. An attraction is [Pha That Luang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pha_That_Luang "Pha That Luang"), a national cultural monument of Laos and 1 of its [stupas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stupa "Stupa"). It was originally built in 1566 by King [Setthathirath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setthathirath "Setthathirath") and was restored in 1953. The golden stupa is 45 metres (148 ft) tall and is believed to contain a relic of the Buddha.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated2-31)

The [Wat Si Muang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Si_Muang "Wat Si Muang") temple was built on the ruins of a Khmer Hindu shrine, the remains of which can be seen behind the [ordination hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordination_hall "Ordination hall").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated3-32) It was built in 1563 and is believed to be guarded by the spirit of a local girl, Nang Si. Legend tells that Nang Si, who was pregnant at the time, leapt to her death as a sacrifice, just as the pillar was being lowered into the hole. In front of the temple stands a statue of King [Sisavang Vong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisavang_Vong "Sisavang Vong").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated3-32)

The memorial monument, [Patuxai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patuxai "Patuxai"), built between 1957 and 1968, is a landmark in the city.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-autogenerated2-31)

[Buddha Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddha_Park "Buddha Park") was built in 1958 by [Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Pu_Bunleua_Sulilat "Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat") and contains a collection of Buddhist and Hindu sculptures, scattered amongst gardens and trees. The park is 28 kilometres (17 mi) south of Vientiane at the edge of the [Mekong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mekong_River "Mekong River").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-33)

Other sites include:

*   [Haw Phra Kaew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haw_Phra_Kaew "Haw Phra Kaew"), former temple, later a museum and shops
*   [Lao National Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_National_Museum "Lao National Museum")
*   [Kaysone Phomvihane Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaysone_Phomvihane_Museum "Kaysone Phomvihane Museum")
*   [Talat Sao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talat_Sao "Talat Sao"), a morning market
*   [That Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That_Dam "That Dam"), a stupa
*   [Wat Ong Teu Mahawihan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Ong_Teu_Mahawihan "Wat Ong Teu Mahawihan"), a Buddhist monastery
*   [Wat Sri Chomphu Ong Tue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Sri_Chomphu_Ong_Tue "Wat Sri Chomphu Ong Tue"), a Buddhist temple
*   [Wat Si Saket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Si_Saket "Wat Si Saket"), a Buddhist temple
*   Wat Sok Pa Luang, a Buddhist temple
*   [Settha Palace Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settha_Palace_Hotel "Settha Palace Hotel"), established 1932
*   The Sanjiang Market[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-34)
*   [Kualao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kualao_Restaurant "Kualao Restaurant"), a restaurant

## Culture

### Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Media")]

Vientiane is the centre of Laos' national media. It hosts the headquarters of[Lao National Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_National_Television "Lao National Television")and[Lao National Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_National_Radio "Lao National Radio"). The city is also served by the municipal broadcaster[VTE9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VTE9?action=edit&redlink=1 "VTE9 (page does not exist)"), as well as[CRI Vientiane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRI_Vientiane "CRI Vientiane"), a station affiliated with [China Radio International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Radio_International "China Radio International").

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

Vientiane has experienced economic growth from foreign investment.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-37) In 2011, the [stock exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_Securities_Exchange "Lao Securities Exchange") opened with two listed company stocks, with the cooperation of [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-38) At the end of 2025, the Laos government announced that the economy of the city had grown by an average of 5.34% per year over the last five years, and that industrial and agricultural shares of the economy declined while the service economy gained in its share of the market.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-39) As of 2026, the economy continues to grow from aforementioned foreign investment, including the private health sector and the [electric vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle "Electric vehicle") sector.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-40) At the beginning of 2026, the Lao government announced an initiative to accrue roughly US$30,000,000 in sought investments[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] to drive the city's economic growth.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-41)

### Bus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Bus")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Vientiane_Bus_-_BRT.jpg/250px-Vientiane_Bus_-_BRT.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vientiane_Bus_-_BRT.jpg)

Vientiane eBRT Bus

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Meter_Taxi_in_Vientiane_01.jpg/250px-Meter_Taxi_in_Vientiane_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meter_Taxi_in_Vientiane_01.jpg)

Older taxis in Vientiane are being replaced by newer Chinese-made cars, like this [Soueast Lioncel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soueast "Soueast").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-42)

There are regular [bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus "Bus") services connecting [Vientiane Bus Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Bus_Station "Vientiane Bus Station") with the rest of the country. In Vientiane, regular bus services around the city are provided by Vientiane Capital State Bus Enterprise.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-43)

Vientiane constructed its first [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) service in 2024 under the Vientiane Urban Transport Project (VSUTP) of Laos' [Ministry of Public Works and Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Public_Works_and_Transport_(Laos) "Ministry of Public Works and Transport (Laos)").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-44) There will be three BRT lines with a total route length of 13.9 km within the capital area. The construction of the BRT was 90% completed in the end of July 2025 and it was scheduled for free trial operation in August 2025, with a total of 55 buses manufactured in China by Chery Wanda;[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-45) it was then delayed to September 2025.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-46) The BRT service officially opened for free trial from 10 March to 9 May 2026; normal fare operation was due to start on 10 May.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-47)

Shortly after the opening of the BRT free trial, the Laos government planned to expand the BRT to [Wattay International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattay_International_Airport "Wattay International Airport") and [China-Laos Vientiane Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_railway_station "Vientiane railway station") in the future. To mitigate the sudden fuel price surge and fuel shortage caused by the [2026 Middle-East conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Iran_War "2026 Iran War"), it is planned to increase the use of electric vehicles in Laos.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-48)

### Rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Rail")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/2a/Laos-China-Railway_Station_Vientiane.jpg/250px-Laos-China-Railway_Station_Vientiane.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laos-China-Railway_Station_Vientiane.jpg)

Vientiane railway station

A [metre gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_gauge "Metre gauge") railway link over the first bridge was formally inaugurated on 5 March 2009, previously ending at [Thanaleng Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanaleng_Railway_Station "Thanaleng Railway Station"), in Dongphosy village ([Vientiane Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Prefecture "Vientiane Prefecture")), 20 km east of Vientiane.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-guardian-09-50) As of November 2010, Lao officials plan to convert the station into a cargo rail terminal for [freight trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freight_trains "Freight trains"), allowing cargo to be transported from Bangkok into Laos more cheaply than via road.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-trweekly-nov10-51)

The [Boten–Vientiane railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boten%E2%80%93Vientiane_railway "Boten–Vientiane railway") (sometimes referred to as the _China–Laos railway_ or _Laos–China railway_) is a 414 kilometres (257 mi)1,435 mm (4 ft 8+1⁄2 in) [standard gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gauge "Standard gauge") electrified railway in [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"), running between the capital Vientiane and the town of [Boten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boten "Boten") on the border with [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). The line was officially opened on 3 December 2021.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-:6-52) In early 2026 the Lao National Assembly approved the first phase of a 562 km standard-gauge railway which will link Vientiane with the Vung Ang deepwater port on Vietnam's coast, providing landlocked Laos direct access to a major port. The project is part of the government's 2026-2030 National Socio-Economic Development Plan.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-53)

### Air

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Air")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/5b/Wattay_Intl_Airport_Vientiane_Laos.jpg/250px-Wattay_Intl_Airport_Vientiane_Laos.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wattay_Intl_Airport_Vientiane_Laos.jpg)

[Wattay International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattay_International_Airport "Wattay International Airport")

Vientiane is served by [Wattay International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattay_International_Airport "Wattay International Airport") with international connections to other Asian destinations such as [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). [Lao Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_Airlines "Lao Airlines") has regular flights to domestic destinations in the country (including flights daily to [Luang Prabang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang "Luang Prabang"), plus flights weekly to other local destinations).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-54)

## Healthcare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vientiane&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Healthcare")]

Main article: [Health in Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_in_Laos "Health in Laos")

The "Centre Medical de l'Ambassade de France" is available to the foreign community in Laos. The [Mahosot Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahosot_Hospital "Mahosot Hospital") is a local hospital in treating and researching diseases and is connected with the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"). In 2011 the Alliance Clinic opened near the airport, with a connection to Thai hospitals. The Setthathirat International Clinic has foreign doctors. A free, 24/7 ambulance service is provided by [Vientiane Rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane_Rescue "Vientiane Rescue"), a volunteer-run rescue service established in 2010.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vientiane#cite_note-55)

**Guangzhou**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-7) also known as **Canton**,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-8) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and largest city of [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong") in [southern China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China "South China").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-9) Located on the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River "Pearl River"), about 120 kilometres (75 mi) northwest of [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") and 145 kilometres (90 mi) north of [Macau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macau "Macau"), Guangzhou has a history of over 2,200 years and was a major terminus of the [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-10)

The [port of Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Guangzhou "Port of Guangzhou") serves as a transportation hub. Guangzhou is also one of China's three largest cities.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-11) For a long time, it was the only Chinese port accessible to the Europeans. Guangzhou was captured by the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") during the [First Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War "First Opium War") and no longer enjoyed a monopoly after the war. Consequently, it lost trade to other ports such as Hong Kong and [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"), but continued to serve as a major [entrepôt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrep%C3%B4t "Entrepôt") at China.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-12)

Guangzhou is at the center of the [Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macau Greater Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong%E2%80%93Hong_Kong%E2%80%93Macau_Greater_Bay_Area "Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macau Greater Bay Area"), the most populous built-up metropolitan region in the world. The area extends into neighboring cities such as [Foshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foshan "Foshan"), [Dongguan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongguan "Dongguan"), [Zhongshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhongshan "Zhongshan"), [Shenzhen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhen "Shenzhen"), parts of [Jiangmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangmen "Jiangmen") and [Huizhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huizhou "Huizhou"), as well as [Zhuhai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhuhai "Zhuhai") and Macau, forming an [urban agglomeration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area") of about 70 million residents.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-13) It is also part of the [Pearl River Delta Economic Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_Delta_Economic_Zone "Pearl River Delta Economic Zone"). Administratively, the city holds [subprovincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-provincial_division "Sub-provincial division") status[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-14) and is one of China's nine [National Central Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Central_City "National Central City").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-15) In the late 1990s and early 2000s, nationals of [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") who had initially settled in the Middle East and Southeast Asia moved in unprecedented numbers to Guangzhou in response to the [1997/98 Asian financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis "1997 Asian financial crisis").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-16) The [domestic migrant population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_in_China "Migration in China") from other [provinces of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_China "Provinces of China") in Guangzhou was 40% of the city's total population in 2008. Guangzhou has one of the most expensive real estate markets in China.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-cnd-17) As of the 2020 census, the registered population of the city's expansive administrative area was 18,676,605 individuals (up 47 percent from the previous census in 2010), of whom 16,492,590 lived in 9 urban districts (all but [Conghua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conghua_District "Conghua District") and [Zengcheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zengcheng_District "Zengcheng District")).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-citypopulation.de-2) Due to worldwide travel restrictions at the beginning of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), [Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou_Baiyun_International_Airport "Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport"), the major airport of Guangzhou, briefly became the [world's busiest airport by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by passenger traffic") in 2020.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-18) Guangzhou is the fifth most populous city by urban resident population in China after Shanghai, [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [Shenzhen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhen "Shenzhen") and [Chongqing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chongqing "Chongqing").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-19)

In modern commerce, Guangzhou is best known for its annual [Canton Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_Fair "Canton Fair"), the oldest and largest [trade fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_fair "Trade fair") in China.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-20) For three consecutive years (2013–2015), Forbes ranked Guangzhou as the best commercial city in mainland China.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-21) Guangzhou is highly ranked as an [Alpha (global first-tier)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network") city together with [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") and [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-22) It is a major [Asia-Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia-Pacific "Asia-Pacific") finance hub, ranking 21st globally in the 2020 [Global Financial Centres Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Financial_Centres_Index "Global Financial Centres Index").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-GFCI-23) Guangzhou also has [the fifth largest number of skyscrapers in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_with_the_most_skyscrapers "List of cities with the most skyscrapers"). As an important international city, Guangzhou has hosted numerous international and national sporting events, the most notable being the [2010 Asian Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Asian_Games "2010 Asian Games"), the [2010 Asian Para Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Asian_Para_Games "2010 Asian Para Games"), and the [2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIBA_Basketball_World_Cup "2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup"). The city hosts 65 [foreign representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diplomatic_missions_in_China#Guangzhou "List of diplomatic missions in China"), making it the major city hosting the third most foreign representatives in China, after Beijing and Shanghai.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-GC-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-CE-25) As of 2020, Guangzhou ranked 10th in the world and 5th in China—after Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen—for the number of billionaire residents by the [Hurun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_Hoogewerf "Rupert Hoogewerf") Global Rich List.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-SS-26) Guangzhou is one of the nation's leading hubs for academia and academic research, [ranking 6th globally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_scientific_output "List of cities by scientific output"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-l2-27) and is home to numerous [Double First-Class Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_First-Class_Construction "Double First-Class Construction"), including [Sun Yat-sen University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Yat-sen_University "Sun Yat-sen University") and [SCUT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_University_of_Technology "South China University of Technology").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-30)

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Guangzhou&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Wuxian_Xiadong.jpg/250px-Wuxian_Xiadong.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wuxian_Xiadong.jpg)

Portrait of the [Grotto of the Five Immortals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grotto_of_the_Five_Immortals "Grotto of the Five Immortals"), the [Taoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoist "Taoist") temple around the five stones which gave Guangzhou its nickname "The City of Rams"

_Guǎngzhōu_ is the official [romanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Chinese "Romanization of Chinese") of the Chinese name 广州 in [Mandarin Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese"). The name of the city is taken from the ancient [Guǎng Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu%C7%8Eng_Prefecture "Guǎng Prefecture") after it had become the prefecture's seat of government. The [character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_character "Chinese character")[廣](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%BB%A3#Traditional_Chinese "wikt:廣") or [广](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%B9%BF#Simplified_Chinese "wikt:广") means 'broad' or 'expansive'.

Before acquiring its current name, the town was known as Panyu (Punyü; [番禺](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%95%AA%E7%A6%BA#Traditional_Chinese "wikt:番禺")), a name still borne by [one of Guangzhou's districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panyu_District "Panyu District") not far from the main city. The origin of the name is still uncertain, with 11 various explanations being offered,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-31) including that it may have referred to two local mountains.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-33) The city has also sometimes been known as Guangzhou Fu or Guangfu after its status as the capital of a [prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu_(administrative_division) "Fu (administrative division)"). From this latter name, Guangzhou was known to medieval Persians such as [Al-Masudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Masudi "Al-Masudi") and [Ibn Khordadbeh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Khordadbeh "Ibn Khordadbeh")[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-34) as Khanfu (خانفو).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-35) Under the [Southern Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Han "Southern Han"), the city was renamed Xingwang Fu (興王府).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-37)

The [Chinese abbreviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_abbreviation "Chinese abbreviation") for Guangzhou is [穗](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%A9%97#Chinese "wikt:穗"), pronounced _Seoi 6_ in Cantonese and _Suì_ in Mandarin—although the abbreviation on car license plates, as with the rest of the province, is [粤](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B2%A4#Simplified_Chinese "wikt:粤")), after its nickname "City of Rice" ([穗城](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%A9%97%E5%9F%8E#Chinese "wikt:穗城")). The city has long borne the nickname City of Rams ([羊城](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%BE%8A%E5%9F%8E#Chinese "wikt:羊城")) or City of the Five Rams ([五羊城](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E4%BA%94%E7%BE%8A%E5%9F%8E#Chinese "wikt:五羊城")) from the five stones at the old [Temple of the Five Immortals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Five_Immortals_(Guangzhou) "Temple of the Five Immortals (Guangzhou)") said to have been the sheep or goats ridden by the [Taoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoism "Taoism")[culture heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_hero "Culture hero") credited with introducing [rice cultivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_cultivation "Rice cultivation") to the area around the time of the city's foundation.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-38) The former name "City of the [Immortals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoist_Immortal "Taoist Immortal")" ([仙城](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E4%BB%99%E5%9F%8E#Chinese "wikt:仙城")/五仙城) came from the same story. The more recent City of Flowers ([花城](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E8%8A%B1%E5%9F%8E#Chinese "wikt:花城")) is usually taken as a simple reference to the area's fine greenery.

The English name "Canton" derived from [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language")_Cidade de Cantão_,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-39) a blend of [dialectal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialects_of_Chinese "Dialects of Chinese") pronunciations of "Guangdong"[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-41) (e.g., [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese")_Gwong2-dung1_). Although it originally and chiefly applied to the walled city, it was occasionally conflated with Guangdong by some authors. It was adopted as the [Postal Map Romanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_Map_Romanization "Postal Map Romanization") of Guangzhou, and remained the official name until its [name change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin") to "Guangzhou". As an adjective, it is still used in describing the [people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese_people "Cantonese people"), [language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese_language "Cantonese language"), [cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese_cuisine "Cantonese cuisine") and [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese_culture "Cantonese culture") of Guangzhou and the surrounding Liangguang region. The 19th-century name was "Kwang-chow foo".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''EB''187837-42)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Guangzhou&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Guangzhou "Timeline of Guangzhou").

### Prehistory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Guangzhou&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Prehistory")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Si_l%C3%BC_yu_yi.JPG/250px-Si_l%C3%BC_yu_yi.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Si_l%C3%BC_yu_yi.JPG)

The [jade burial suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jade_burial_suit "Jade burial suit") of [Zhao Mo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Mo "Zhao Mo") in Guangzhou's [Nanyue King Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanyue_King_Museum "Nanyue King Museum")

Prior to the [Han conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_conquest_of_Nanyue "Han conquest of Nanyue"), the area of modern Guangzhou was inhabited by indigenous, non-Chinese tribes known collectively as the [Baiyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baiyue "Baiyue").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-43)

A settlement now known as Nanwucheng was present in the area by 1100 BC.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-45) Some traditional Chinese histories placed Nanwucheng's founding during the reign of [King Nan of Zhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Nan_of_Zhou "King Nan of Zhou"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-anatomy-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-acc-47)[emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Zhou_emperors "List of Zhou emperors") of [Zhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_dynasty "Zhou dynasty") from 314 to 256 BC. It was said to have consisted of little more than a stockade of bamboo and mud.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-anatomy-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-acc-47)

### Nanyue

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Guangzhou&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Nanyue")]

Guangzhou, then known as **Panyu**, was founded on the eastern bank of the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(China) "Pearl River (China)") in 214 BC.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''EB''187837-42) Ships commanded by [tradespersons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tradesperson "Tradesperson") arrived on the South China coast in the late [antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquities "Antiquities"). Surviving records from the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") confirm, that the residents of Panyu observed a range of trade missions. Records on foreign trade ships reach upon til the late 20th century.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-48)

Panyu was the seat of [Qin Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_Empire "Qin Empire")'s [Nanhai Commandery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanhai_Commandery "Nanhai Commandery"), and served as a base for the [first invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_conquest_of_Guangdong "Qin conquest of Guangdong") of the [Baiyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baiyue "Baiyue") lands in southern China. Legendary accounts claimed that the soldiers at Panyu were so vigilant that they did not remove their armor for three years.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-49) Upon the [fall of the Qin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Qin "Fall of the Qin"), General [Zhao Tuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Tuo "Zhao Tuo") established the kingdom of [Nanyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanyue "Nanyue") and made Panyu its capital in 204 BC. It remained independent throughout the [Chu-Han Contention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chu-Han_Contention "Chu-Han Contention"), although Zhao negotiated recognition of his independence in exchange for his nominal submission to the [Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") in 196 BC.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-50) Archeological evidence shows that Panyu was an expansive commercial center: in addition to items from central China, archeologists have found remains originating from [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), India, and even Africa.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-51) Zhao Tuo was succeeded by [Zhao Mo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Mo "Zhao Mo") and then Zhao Yingqi. Upon [Zhao Yingqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Yingqi "Zhao Yingqi")'s death in 115 BC, his younger son [Zhao Xing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Xing "Zhao Xing") was named as his successor in violation of Chinese [primogeniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primogeniture "Primogeniture"). By 113 BC, his [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_people "Han people") mother, the Empress Dowager Jiu ([樛](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E6%A8%9B "wikt:樛")) had prevailed upon him to submit Nanyue as a formal part of the Han Empire. The native [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_councillor "Grand councillor")[Lü Jia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BC_Jia_(Nanyue) "Lü Jia (Nanyue)") launched a coup, killing Han ambassadors along with the king, his mother, and their supporters.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEY%C3%BC1987453-52) A successful ambush then annihilated a Han force which had been sent to arrest him. [Emperor Wu of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Wu_of_Han "Emperor Wu of Han") took offense and launched [a massive riverine and seaborne war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han%E2%80%93Nanyue_War "Han–Nanyue War"): six armies under [Lu Bode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lu_Bode "Lu Bode") and Yang Pu[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-53) took Panyu and annexed Nanyue by the end of 111 BC.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEY%C3%BC1987453-52)

### Imperial China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Guangzhou&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Imperial China")]

Incorporated into the [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Han_dynasty "Western Han dynasty"), Panyu became a provincial capital. In AD 226, it became the seat of Guang [Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_(country_subdivision) "Zhou (country subdivision)"), which gave it its modern name. The _[Old Book of Tang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old\_Book\_of\_Tang "Old Book of Tang")_ described Guangzhou as an important port in southern China.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-54) Direct routes connected the Middle East and China, as shown in the records of a Chinese prisoner returning home from Iraq twelve years after his capture at [Talas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Talas "Battle of Talas").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-55) Relations were often strained: while China was undergoing the [An Lushan Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion "An Lushan Rebellion"), Arab and Persian pirates[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-IH-56)[sacked the city on 30 October 758](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Guangzhou_(758) "Sack of Guangzhou (758)")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-bret-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-welsh-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-need-59)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-sima-60) and in revenge thousands of Arabs and Persians were killed by Chinese rebels in the [Yangzhou massacre (760)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangzhou_massacre_(760) "Yangzhou massacre (760)"). In the [Guangzhou massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou_massacre "Guangzhou massacre") about 200,000 Arab, Persian and other foreigners were killed by Chinese rebel [Huang Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huang_Chao "Huang Chao") in 878, along with the city's [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews"), [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-frenchy-61)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-kaifung-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-gibberish-63) and [Parsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsi "Parsi").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-sirafi-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-guy-65) The port was closed for fifty years after its destruction.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-IH-56)

Amid the [Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Dynasties_and_Ten_Kingdoms "Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms") that followed the collapse of the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"), the [Later Liang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Later_Liang_(Five_Dynasties) "Later Liang (Five Dynasties)") governor [Liu Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Yan_(emperor) "Liu Yan (emperor)") used his base at Panyu to establish a "Great Yue" or "[Southern Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Han "Southern Han")" empire, which lasted from 917 to 971. The region enjoyed considerable cultural and economic success in this period. From the 10th to 12th century, there are records that the large foreign communities were not exclusively men, but included "[Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_people "Persian people") females".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-67) According to [Odoric of Pordenone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoric_of_Pordenone "Odoric of Pordenone"), Guangzhou was as large as three Venices in terms of area, and rivaled all of Italy in the amount of crafts produced. He also noted the large amount of ginger available as well as large geese and snakes.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYule2002121-68) Guangzhou was visited by the [Moroccan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_people "Moroccan people") traveler [Ibn Battuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Battuta "Ibn Battuta") during his journey around the world in the 14th century.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunn1986259-69) He detailed the process by which the Chinese constructed their large ships in the port's shipyards.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-70)

Shortly after the [Hongwu Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hongwu_Emperor "Hongwu Emperor")'s declaration of the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty"), he reversed his earlier support of [foreign trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_trade "Foreign trade") and imposed the first of a series of [sea bans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haijin "Haijin").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-71) These banned private foreign trade upon penalty of death for the merchant and exile for his family and neighbors.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi20103-72) Previous maritime intendancies of Guangzhou, [Quanzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quanzhou "Quanzhou"), and [Ningbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ningbo "Ningbo") were closed in 1384[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn1996116-73) and legal trade became limited to the [tribute delegations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Chinese_tributary_system "Imperial Chinese tributary system") sent to or by official representatives of foreign governments.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199691-74)
