The name of the territory, first [romanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization "Romanization") as "He-Ong-Kong" in 1780,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-33) originally referred to a small inlet located between [Aberdeen Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ap_Lei_Chau "Ap Lei Chau") and the southern coast of Hong Kong Island. [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen,_Hong_Kong "Aberdeen, Hong Kong") was an initial point of contact between British sailors and local fishermen.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-34) Although the source of the romanised name is unknown, it is generally believed to be an early phonetic rendering of the [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese") (or [Tanka Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanka_people#Dialect "Tanka people")) phrase _hēung góng_. The name translates as "fragrant harbour" or "incense harbour".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-HerbariumName-31)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-CarrollHKName-32)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-etym-35) "Fragrant" may refer to the sweet taste of the harbour's freshwater influx from the Pearl River or to the odour from incense factories lining the coast of northern [Kowloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon "Kowloon"). The incense was stored near Aberdeen Harbour for export before [Victoria Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Harbour "Victoria Harbour") was developed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-etym-35)[Sir John Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Davis "John Francis Davis") (the second colonial governor) offered an alternative origin; Davis said that the name derived from "Hoong-keang" ("red torrent"), reflecting the colour of soil over which a waterfall on the island flowed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-36)

The simplified name _Hong Kong_ was frequently used by 1810.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-37) The name was also commonly written as the single word _Hongkong_ until 1926, when the government officially adopted the two-word name.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-38) Some corporations founded during the early colonial era still keep this name, including [Hongkong Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hongkong_Land "Hongkong Land"), [Hongkong Electric Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hongkong_Electric_Company "Hongkong Electric Company"), [Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hongkong_and_Shanghai_Hotels "Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels"), and [the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hongkong_and_Shanghai_Banking_Corporation "The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation") (HSBC).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-39)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-HSBC-40)

## History

Main article: [History of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Hong_Kong "History of Hong Kong")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Hong Kong history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Hong_Kong_history "Timeline of Hong Kong history").

### Prehistory and Imperial China

The earliest known human traces in what is now called Hong Kong are dated by some to 35,000-39,000 years ago during the [Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic "Paleolithic") period. The claim is based on an archaeological investigation in [Wong Tei Tung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wong_Tei_Tung "Wong Tei Tung") in the [Sai Kung Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sai_Kung_Peninsula "Sai Kung Peninsula") in 2003. The archaeological works revealed [knapped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knapping "Knapping")[stone tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_tool "Stone tool") from deposits dated by optical [luminescence dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminescence_dating "Luminescence dating").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-41)

During the Middle [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") period, about 6,000 years ago, the region had been widely occupied by humans.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Meacham2-42) Neolithic to [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") Hong Kong settlers were semi-coastal people. Early inhabitants are believed to have been [Austronesians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austronesian_peoples "Austronesian peoples") in the Middle Neolithic period, and later the [Yue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baiyue "Baiyue") people.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Meacham2-42) As hinted by the archaeological works in Sha Ha, Sai Kung, rice cultivation had been introduced since the [Late Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Neolithic "Late Neolithic") period.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Li38-43) Bronze Age Hong Kong featured coarse pottery, hard pottery, quartz and stone jewelry, as well as small bronze implements.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Meacham2-42)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Sung_Wong_Toi.jpg/250px-Sung_Wong_Toi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sung_Wong_Toi.jpg)

[Sung Wong Toi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sung_Wong_Toi "Sung Wong Toi")

The [Qin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty") incorporated the Hong Kong area into China for the first time in 214 BCE, after [conquering the indigenous Baiyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_campaign_against_the_Yue_tribes "Qin campaign against the Yue tribes").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-44) The region was consolidated under the [Nanyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanyue "Nanyue") kingdom (a predecessor state of [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam")) after the Qin collapse,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-KeatGinOoi-45) and it was recaptured by China after the [Han conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_conquest_of_Nanyue "Han conquest of Nanyue").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-46) During the [Mongol conquest of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_conquest_of_the_Song_dynasty "Mongol conquest of the Song dynasty") in the 13th century, the [southern Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_dynasty "Song dynasty") court was briefly located in modern-day [Kowloon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_City "Kowloon City") (the [Sung Wong Toi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sung_Wong_Toi "Sung Wong Toi") site) before its final defeat in the 1279 [Battle of Yamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Yamen "Battle of Yamen") by the [Yuan dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty "Yuan dynasty").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Barber-47) By the end of the Yuan dynasty, seven large families had settled in the region and owned most of the land. Settlers from nearby provinces migrated to Kowloon throughout the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-48)

The earliest known European visitor was [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") explorer [Jorge Álvares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_%C3%81lvares "Jorge Álvares"), who arrived in 1513.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-49)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-50) Portuguese merchants established a trading post called [Tamão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tam%C3%A3o "Tamão") in Hong Kong waters and began regular trade with southern China. Although the traders were expelled after [military clashes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tunmen "Battle of Tunmen") in the 1520s,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-51) Portuguese-Chinese trade relations were [re-established by 1549](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luso-Chinese_agreement "Luso-Chinese agreement"). Portugal acquired a [permanent lease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Portuguese_Treaty_of_Peking "Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking") for [Macau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macau "Macau") in 1887.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-52)

After the [Qing conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_from_Ming_to_Qing "Transition from Ming to Qing"), maritime trade was banned under the _[Haijin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haijin "Haijin")_ policies. From 1661 to 1683, the population of most of the area that forms present-day Hong Kong was cleared under the [Great Clearance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Clearance "Great Clearance"), turning the region into a wasteland.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-HK_story-53) The [Kangxi Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangxi_Emperor "Kangxi Emperor") lifted the maritime trade prohibition, allowing foreigners to enter Chinese ports in 1684.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-54) Qing authorities established the [Canton System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_System "Canton System") in 1757 to regulate trade more strictly, restricting non-Russian ships to the port of Canton.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-55) Although European demand for Chinese commodities like tea, silk, and porcelain was high, Chinese interest in European manufactured goods was insignificant, so that Chinese goods could only be bought with precious metals. To reduce the trade imbalance, the British sold large amounts of Indian [opium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium "Opium") to China. Faced with a drug crisis, Qing officials pursued ever more aggressive actions to halt the opium trade.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-56)

### British colony

Main article: [British Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Hong_Kong "British Hong Kong")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Hong_Kong_1868.jpg/250px-Hong_Kong_1868.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hong_Kong_1868.jpg)

Hong Kong in 1868, photograph by [John Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Thomson_(photographer) "John Thomson (photographer)")

In 1839, the [Daoguang Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daoguang_Emperor "Daoguang Emperor") rejected proposals to legalise and tax [opium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium "Opium") and ordered imperial commissioner [Lin Zexu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lin_Zexu "Lin Zexu") to eradicate the opium trade. The commissioner destroyed opium stockpiles and halted all foreign trade,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-57) triggering a British military response and the [First Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War "First Opium War"). The Qing surrendered early in the war and ceded Hong Kong Island in the [Convention of Chuenpi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_of_Chuenpi "Convention of Chuenpi"), signed by [Charles Elliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Elliot "Charles Elliot") and [Qishan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qishan_(official) "Qishan (official)"). British forces began controlling Hong Kong shortly after the signing of the convention, on 26 January 1841.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-58) However, both countries were dissatisfied and did not ratify the agreement.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-59) After more than a year of further hostilities, Hong Kong Island was formally ceded to the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") in the 1842 [Treaty of Nanking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Nanking "Treaty of Nanking").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Courtauld-60)

Administrative infrastructure was quickly built by early 1842, but piracy, disease, and hostile Qing policies initially prevented the government from attracting commerce. Conditions on the island improved during the [Taiping Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiping_Rebellion "Taiping Rebellion") in the 1850s, when many Chinese refugees, including wealthy merchants, fled mainland turbulence and settled in the colony.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-CarrollEarlyHistory-22) Further tensions between the British and Qing over the opium trade escalated into the [Second Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Opium_War "Second Opium War"). The Qing were again defeated and were forced to give up [Kowloon Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Peninsula "Kowloon Peninsula") and [Stonecutters Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonecutters_Island "Stonecutters Island") in the [Convention of Peking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_of_Peking "Convention of Peking").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-SecondOpiumWar-61) By the end of this war, Hong Kong had evolved from a transient colonial outpost into a major [entrepôt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrep%C3%B4t "Entrepôt"). Rapid economic improvement during the 1850s attracted foreign investment, as potential stakeholders became more confident in Hong Kong's future.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-62)

The colony was further expanded in 1898 when the United Kingdom obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-NTLease-63) The [University of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hong_Kong "University of Hong Kong") was established in 1911 as the territory's first institution of higher education.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-64)[Kai Tak Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kai_Tak_Airport "Kai Tak Airport") began operation in 1924, and the colony avoided a prolonged economic downturn after the 1925–26 [Canton–Hong Kong strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton%E2%80%93Hong_Kong_strike "Canton–Hong Kong strike").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-KaiTak-65)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-66) At the start of the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War") in 1937, Governor [Geoffry Northcote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffry_Northcote "Geoffry Northcote") declared Hong Kong a neutral zone to safeguard its status as a free port.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-67) The colonial government prepared for a possible attack, evacuating all British women and children in 1940.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-68) The [Imperial Japanese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Army "Imperial Japanese Army")[attacked Hong Kong on 8 December 1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hong_Kong "Battle of Hong Kong"), the same morning as its [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor "Attack on Pearl Harbor").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-69) Hong Kong was [occupied by Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_occupation_of_Hong_Kong "Japanese occupation of Hong Kong") for almost four years before the British resumed control on 30 August 1945.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-70)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Flag_of_Hong_Kong_%281959%E2%80%931997%29.svg/250px-Flag_of_Hong_Kong_%281959%E2%80%931997%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_Hong_Kong_1959.svg)

The [flag of British Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Hong_Kong_(1871%E2%80%931997) "Flag of Hong Kong (1871–1997)") from 1959 to 1997

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/578a_Hong_Kong_1971_%2851321892645%29.jpg/250px-578a_Hong_Kong_1971_%2851321892645%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:578a_Hong_Kong_1971_(51321892645).jpg)

[Peking Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Road "Peking Road") in Tsim Sha Tsui in 1971

Its population rebounded quickly after the war, as skilled Chinese migrants fled from the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War") and more refugees crossed the border when the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") took control of mainland China in 1949.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Wiltshire-71) Hong Kong became the first of the [Four Asian Tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Asian_Tigers "Four Asian Tigers") economies to industrialise during the 1950s.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-72) With a rapidly increasing population, the colonial government attempted reforms to improve infrastructure and public services. The [public-housing estate programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_housing_in_Hong_Kong "Public housing in Hong Kong"), [Independent Commission Against Corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Commission_Against_Corruption_(Hong_Kong) "Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong)"), and [Mass Transit Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTR "MTR") were all established during the post-war decades to provide safer housing, integrity in the civil service, and more reliable transportation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-73)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-74)

Nevertheless, widespread public discontent led to multiple protests from the 1950s to 1980s, including pro-[Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") and pro-[Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") demonstrations. In the [1967 Hong Kong riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Hong_Kong_riots "1967 Hong Kong riots"), pro-[PRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") protestors clashed with the British colonial government. As many as 51 were killed, and 802 were injured in the violence, including dozens killed by the [Royal Hong Kong Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Hong_Kong_Police "Royal Hong Kong Police") via beatings and shootings.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-75)

Although the territory's manufacturing competitiveness gradually declined due to rising labour and property costs, it transitioned to a service-based economy. By the early 1990s, Hong Kong had established itself as a global [financial centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_centre "Financial centre") and shipping hub.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-76)

### Chinese special administrative region

Further information: [Handover of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handover_of_Hong_Kong "Handover of Hong Kong")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Avenue_of_Stars%2C_Hong_Kong_%282052819038%29.jpg/250px-Avenue_of_Stars%2C_Hong_Kong_%282052819038%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Avenue_of_Stars,_Hong_Kong_(2052819038).jpg)

[Victoria Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Harbour "Victoria Harbour") and [Hong Kong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Island "Hong Kong Island"), 2007

The colony faced an uncertain future as the end of the New Territories lease approached, and [Governor Murray MacLehose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_MacLehose,_Baron_MacLehose_of_Beoch "Murray MacLehose, Baron MacLehose of Beoch") raised the question of Hong Kong's status with [Deng Xiaoping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping") in 1979.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-77) Diplomatic negotiations with China resulted in the 1984 [Sino-British Joint Declaration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-British_Joint_Declaration "Sino-British Joint Declaration"), in which the United Kingdom agreed to the handover of the colony in 1997, and China would guarantee Hong Kong's economic and political systems for 50 years after the handover.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Carroll181-78) The impending handover triggered a [wave of mass emigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waves_of_mass_migrations_from_Hong_Kong "Waves of mass migrations from Hong Kong") as residents feared an erosion of civil rights, the rule of law, and quality of life.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-79) Over half a million people left the territory during the peak migration period, from 1987 to 1996.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-2002Pop-80) The Legislative Council became a [fully elected legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "1995 Hong Kong legislative election") for the first time in 1995. It extensively expanded its functions and organisations throughout the last years of the colonial rule.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-81) The handover of Hong Kong to China was at midnight on 1 July 1997, after 156 years of British rule.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-NYTHandover-82)

Immediately after the handover, Hong Kong was severely affected by several crises. The Hong Kong government was forced to use substantial [foreign exchange reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_exchange_reserves "Foreign exchange reserves") to maintain the Hong Kong dollar's currency peg during the [1997 Asian financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis "1997 Asian financial crisis"),[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Wiltshire-71) and the recovery from this was muted by an [H5N1 avian-flu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influenza_A_virus_subtype_H5N1 "Influenza A virus subtype H5N1") outbreak[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-83) and a housing surplus.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-84) This was followed by the [2003 SARS epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002%E2%80%932004_SARS_outbreak "2002–2004 SARS outbreak"), during which the territory experienced its most serious economic downturn.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-85)

Chinese communists portrayed the return of Hong Kong as a key moment in the PRC's rise to [great power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_power "Great power") status.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-:172-86):51

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Hong_Kong_anti-extradition_bill_protest_%2848108527758%29.jpg/250px-Hong_Kong_anti-extradition_bill_protest_%2848108527758%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hong_Kong_anti-extradition_bill_protest_(48108527758).jpg)

[Hong Kong protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%932020_Hong_Kong_protests "2019–2020 Hong Kong protests"), August 2019

Political debates after the handover have centred around the region's [democratic development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_development_in_Hong_Kong "Democratic development in Hong Kong") and the [Chinese central government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "State Council of the People's Republic of China")'s adherence to the "one country, two systems" principle. After reversal of the last colonial era Legislative Council [democratic reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Hong_Kong_electoral_reform "1994 Hong Kong electoral reform") following the handover,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-87) the regional government unsuccessfully attempted to enact [national security legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_(Legislative_Provisions)_Bill_2003 "National Security (Legislative Provisions) Bill 2003") pursuant to [Article 23 of the Basic Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Basic_Law_Article_23 "Hong Kong Basic Law Article 23").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-88) The central government decision to implement [nominee pre-screening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NPCSC_Decision_on_Hong_Kong "2014 NPCSC Decision on Hong Kong") before allowing [chief executive elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%932015_Hong_Kong_electoral_reform "2014–2015 Hong Kong electoral reform") triggered a series of [protests in 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Hong_Kong_protests "2014 Hong Kong protests") which became known as the Umbrella Revolution.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-89) Discrepancies in the electoral registry and disqualification of elected legislators after the [2016 Legislative Council elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "2016 Hong Kong legislative election")[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-90)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-91)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-92) and enforcement of national law in the [West Kowloon high-speed railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_West_Kowloon_railway_station "Hong Kong West Kowloon railway station") raised further concerns about the region's autonomy.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-93) In June 2019, [mass protests erupted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%932020_Hong_Kong_protests "2019–2020 Hong Kong protests") in response to a [proposed extradition amendment bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Hong_Kong_extradition_bill "2019 Hong Kong extradition bill") permitting the extradition of fugitives to mainland China. The protests are the largest in Hong Kong's history,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-EconomistRestoreCalm-94) with organisers claiming to have attracted more than three million Hong Kong residents.

#### Following the 2019 protests

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Hong_Kong_Tramways_103%28Z05%29_Shau_Kei_Wan_to_Happy_Valley_06-07-2020.jpg/250px-Hong_Kong_Tramways_103%28Z05%29_Shau_Kei_Wan_to_Happy_Valley_06-07-2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hong_Kong_Tramways_103(Z05)_Shau_Kei_Wan_to_Happy_Valley_06-07-2020.jpg)

A tram with slogans promoting the National Security Law printed on it

The Hong Kong regional government and the Chinese central government responded to the protests with many administrative measures to quell dissent. In June 2020, the Legislative Council passed the [National Anthem Ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Anthem_Ordinance "National Anthem Ordinance"), which criminalised "insults to the national anthem of China".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-95) The Chinese central government meanwhile enacted the [Hong Kong national security law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Hong_Kong_national_security_law "2020 Hong Kong national security law") to help quell protests in the region.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-cnn20200630-96) Nine months later, in March 2021, the Chinese central government introduced [amendments to Hong Kong's electoral system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Hong_Kong_electoral_changes "2021 Hong Kong electoral changes"), which included the reduction of directly elected seats in the Legislative Council and the requirement that all candidates be vetted and approved by a Beijing-appointed [Candidate Eligibility Review Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidate_Eligibility_Review_Committee "Candidate Eligibility Review Committee").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-france2420210311-97)

In July 2023, [Hong Kong's Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Council_of_Hong_Kong "Legislative Council of Hong Kong") passed reforms slashing directly elected [District Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Council_Eligibility_Review_Committee "District Council Eligibility Review Committee") seats and establishing a vetting committee for candidates.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-dc2023_freepress01-98)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-dc2023_gld01-99)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-dc2023_gld02-100)

In terms of international connectedness, as of 2024, the city was one of eight worldwide that was classified as an "Alpha+" city by the [Globalization and World Cities Research Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-101)

## Government and politics

Main articles: [Government of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Hong_Kong "Government of Hong Kong"), [Politics of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Hong_Kong "Politics of Hong Kong"), [Elections in Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Hong_Kong "Elections in Hong Kong"), and [Separation of powers in Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_powers_in_Hong_Kong "Separation of powers in Hong Kong")

[![Image 25: Large, round room with desks and a dais](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Legco_Complex_Chamber_20240420.jpg/250px-Legco_Complex_Chamber_20240420.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Legco_Complex_Chamber_20240420.jpg)

Since 2012, the legislature has met in the [Tamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar,_Hong_Kong "Tamar, Hong Kong")[Legislative Council Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Council_Complex "Legislative Council Complex").

Hong Kong is a [special administrative region of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_administrative_regions_of_China "Special administrative regions of China"), with executive, legislative, and judicial powers [devolved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devolution "Devolution") from the [national government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-102) The Sino-British Joint Declaration provided for economic and administrative continuity through the handover,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Carroll181-78) resulting in an [executive-led](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government) "Executive (government)") governing system largely inherited from the territory's history as a British colony.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-BasicLaw15-103) Under these terms and the "one country, two systems" principle, the [Basic Law of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Basic_Law "Hong Kong Basic Law") is the regional constitution.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-104) The regional government is composed of three branches:

*   _[Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government\_of\_Hong\_Kong "Government of Hong Kong"):_ As Hong Kong operates under an executive-led system, the [Chief Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Executive_of_Hong_Kong "Chief Executive of Hong Kong") is responsible for enforcing regional law,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-BasicLaw15-103) can force reconsideration of legislation,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-105) and appoints [Executive Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Council_of_Hong_Kong "Executive Council of Hong Kong") members and [principal officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_officials_of_Hong_Kong "Principal officials of Hong Kong").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-106) Acting with the Executive Council, the [Chief Executive-in-Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King-in-Council#The_Commonwealth "King-in-Council") can propose new bills, issue [subordinate legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_and_secondary_legislation "Primary and secondary legislation"), and has authority to [dissolve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_parliament "Dissolution of parliament") the legislature.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-107) In [states of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") or public danger, the [Chief Executive-in-Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Executive-in-Council "Chief Executive-in-Council") is further [empowered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_Regulations_Ordinance "Emergency Regulations Ordinance") to enact any regulation necessary to restore public order.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-108)
*   _[Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative\_Council\_of\_Hong\_Kong "Legislative Council of Hong Kong"):_ The unicameral [Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Council_of_Hong_Kong "Legislative Council of Hong Kong") enacts regional law, approves budgets, and has the power to [impeach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment "Impeachment") a sitting chief executive.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-109)
*   _[Judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary\_of\_Hong\_Kong "Judiciary of Hong Kong"):_ The [Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Court_of_Final_Appeal "Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal") and lower courts interpret laws and overturn those inconsistent with the Basic Law.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Gittings150-110) The chief executive appoints judges on the advice of a recommendation commission.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-111)

The chief executive is the [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government "Head of government"), serving for a maximum of two five-year terms; however, as of 2026, no chief executive has completed the maximum two five-year term limit.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-112) The [State Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_China "State Council of China") (led by the [Premier of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_China "Premier of China")) appoints the chief executive after nomination by the [Election Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Committee "Election Committee"), which is composed of 1500 business, community, and government leaders.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-113)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-114)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-115)

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Hong_Kong_Government_House_08-09-2024%281%29.jpg/250px-Hong_Kong_Government_House_08-09-2024%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hong_Kong_Government_House_08-09-2024(1).jpg)

Hong Kong Government House

The Legislative Council has 90 members, each serving a four-year term. Twenty are directly elected from [geographical constituencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographical_constituency "Geographical constituency"), thirty represent [functional constituencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_constituency_(Hong_Kong) "Functional constituency (Hong Kong)") (FC), and forty are chosen by an [election committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Committee_(constituency) "Election Committee (constituency)") consisting of representatives appointed by the Chinese central government.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-overhaul_HK-116) Thirty FC councillors are selected from limited electorates representing sectors of the economy or special interest groups.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-LegCoVoting-117) Geographical constituency elected members are chosen by single non-transferable vote ([SNTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_non-transferable_vote "Single non-transferable vote")), yielding two candidates per GC. The 30 limited electorate functional constituencies fill their seats using [first-past-the-post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting "First-past-the-post voting") or [instant-runoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting "Instant-runoff voting") voting.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-LegCoVoting-117)

Twenty-two political parties had representatives elected to the Legislative Council in the [2016 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "2016 Hong Kong legislative election").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-118) These parties have aligned themselves into three ideological groups: the [pro-Beijing camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-Beijing_camp_(Hong_Kong) "Pro-Beijing camp (Hong Kong)") (the current government), the [pro-democracy camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-democracy_camp_(Hong_Kong) "Pro-democracy camp (Hong Kong)"), and [localist groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Localism_in_Hong_Kong "Localism in Hong Kong").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-119) However, by [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "2021 Hong Kong legislative election"), the pro-democracy camp and the localist groups lost all representation in the Legislative Council as a result of the [2021 electoral changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Hong_Kong_electoral_changes "2021 Hong Kong electoral changes") imposed by the [National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress"),[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-120) and since [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "2025 Hong Kong legislative election") all 90 members of the Legislative Council have been from the pro-Beijing camp. The Chinese Communist Party does not have an official political presence in Hong Kong, and its members do not run in local elections.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-121) Hong Kong is represented in the National People's Congress by 36 deputies chosen through an electoral college and 203 delegates in the [National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Committee_of_the_Chinese_People's_Political_Consultative_Conference "National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference") appointed by the central government.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-NationalReps-10)

[![Image 27: The grey dome and front gable of a granite neo-classical building, with a skyscraper in the background against a clear blue sky](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Court_of_Final_Appeal_Building.jpg/250px-Court_of_Final_Appeal_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Court_of_Final_Appeal_Building.jpg)

The [Court of Final Appeal Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Final_Appeal_Building "Court of Final Appeal Building") formerly housed the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_(Hong_Kong) "Supreme Court (Hong Kong)") and the [Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Council_of_Hong_Kong "Legislative Council of Hong Kong").

There are major differences between Hong Kong's legal system and the rest of China's.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-Gittings150-110) Its judicial system is based on [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law "Common law"), continuing the legal tradition established during British rule.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-122) Local courts may refer to precedents set in [English law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_law "English law") and overseas jurisprudence.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-123) However, [mainland criminal procedure law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Procedure_Law_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Criminal Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China") applies to cases investigated by the [Office for Safeguarding National Security of the CPG in the HKSAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_for_Safeguarding_National_Security "Office for Safeguarding National Security").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-NPC_Observer-124) Interpretative and amending power over the Basic Law and jurisdiction over acts of state lie with the central authority, making regional courts ultimately subordinate to the mainland's [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_law "Socialist law")[civil law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_(legal_system) "Civil law (legal system)") system.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-125) Decisions made by the [Standing Committee **Hong Kong**[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-20) is a [special administrative region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_administrative_regions_of_China "Special administrative regions of China") of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). Situated on China's southern coast just south of [Shenzhen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhen "Shenzhen"), it consists of [Hong Kong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Island "Hong Kong Island"), [Kowloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon "Kowloon"), and the [New Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Territories "New Territories"). With 7.5 million residents in a 1,114-square-kilometre (430 sq mi) territory, Hong Kong is the [fourth-most densely populated region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density") in the world.

Hong Kong was established as a [colony of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Hong_Kong "British Hong Kong") after the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") ceded [Hong Kong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Island "Hong Kong Island") in 1841–1842 as a result of losing the [First Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War "First Opium War"). The colony expanded to the [Kowloon Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Peninsula "Kowloon Peninsula") in 1860 and was further extended when the United Kingdom obtained a [99-year lease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/99-year_lease "99-year lease") of the New Territories in 1898. Hong Kong was [occupied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_occupation_of_Hong_Kong "Japanese occupation of Hong Kong") by [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") from [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hong_Kong "Battle of Hong Kong") to [1945](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_Day_(Hong_Kong) "Liberation Day (Hong Kong)") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The territory was [handed over from the United Kingdom to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handover_of_Hong_Kong "Handover of Hong Kong") in 1997. Hong Kong maintains separate governing and economic systems from those of [mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") under the principle of [one country, two systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_country,_two_systems "One country, two systems").[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-21)

Originally an area of farming and fishing villages,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-CarrollEarlyHistory-22)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-FOOTNOTERen2010221-23) Hong Kong is now one of the world's most significant [financial centres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_centre "Financial centre") and [commercial ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_port "Commercial port"). Hong Kong is the world's [third-ranked global financial centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Financial_Centres_Index "Global Financial Centres Index") behind [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), the ninth-largest exporter, and the eighth-largest importer in the world. Its currency, the [Hong Kong dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_dollar "Hong Kong dollar"), is the [ninth-most traded currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Most_traded_currencies "Template:Most traded currencies") globally. Home to the [third-highest number of billionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_number_of_billionaires "List of cities by number of billionaires") of any city in the world, Hong Kong has the second largest number of [ultra high-net-worth individuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_high-net-worth_individual "Ultra high-net-worth individual").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-24)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-25)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-26)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-27) The city has one of the highest [per capita incomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita"), although severe [income inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_income_equality "List of countries by income equality") still exists among the population.

Hong Kong is [the region with the most skyscrapers in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_with_the_most_skyscrapers "List of cities with the most skyscrapers"). [Housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_in_Hong_Kong "Housing in Hong Kong") is consistently in high demand, making the city of Hong Kong the most expensive residential property market in the world and one of the [most expensive cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_cities_for_expatriate_employees "List of most expensive cities for expatriate employees") in the world.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-28)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-29)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong#cite_note-30) It is also one of [the most visited cities in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_international_visitors "List of cities by international visitors").

Hong Kong is a [highly developed territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country") and has a [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index") (HDI) of 0.955, [ranking eighth in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by Human Development Index"), and is currently the only place in Asia to be in the top ten. Hong Kong is categorized as an [Alpha+ city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_city "Global city") by the [Globalization and World Cities Research Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network"). The city has the [highest life expectancy in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy "List of countries by life expectancy"), and has a [public transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_in_Hong_Kong "Transport in Hong Kong") usage exceeding 90 percent.
