**Lane Crawford (HK) Limited** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"):連卡佛) is a retail company founded in 1850 operating specialist department stores selling luxury goods in Hong Kong and Mainland China.[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-reuters2008-1) It is headquartered in [One Island South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Island_South?action=edit&redlink=1 "One Island South (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/One%20Island%20South "zh:One Island South")], [Wong Chuk Hang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wong_Chuk_Hang "Wong Chuk Hang").[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-2)

Lane Crawford is a part of the Lane Crawford Joyce Group, which also owns the fashion retailer, [Joyce Boutique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyce_Boutique "Joyce Boutique").[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lane_Crawford&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lane_Crawford&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

In August 1850, two [Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scot "Scot"), Thomas Ash Lane and Ninian Crawford opened a shop in a makeshift bamboo structure on the waterfront at the present location of [Des Voeux Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Voeux_Road "Des Voeux Road").[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-4) Taking each of their individual surnames, Lane Crawford later occupied a number of retail sites along Des Voeux Road and [Queen's Road Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Road_Central "Queen's Road Central"). In the early 1900s, it expanded with stores in Guangzhou and Shanghai in China, and [Kobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobe "Kobe") and Tokyo in Japan.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-:0-5) It offered services including a tailor and outfitter, a draper, a provisions dealer, a wine and spirits merchant, an auctioneer of antiques, a baker, a restaurant, as well as a bar.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-6)

During the [Japanese Occupation of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_occupation_of_Hong_Kong "Japanese occupation of Hong Kong") between 1941 and 1945, all Lane Crawford properties and assets were taken over by the Japanese Authorities, who transferred the store's operations to the Japanese chain, [Matsuzakaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuzakaya "Matsuzakaya").[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-:0-5)[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-7)

Following damages resulting from the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War"), Lane Crawford had to rebuild from scratch, so it began expanding its import-export division from foodstuffs to luxury items such as cosmetics and [pearls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearls "Pearls"). By 1975, jewellers accounted for 42 percent of sales.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-:0-5)

### Present

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lane_Crawford&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Present")]

In 2004, Lane Crawford opened a revamped retail store at [IFC Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IFC_Mall_(Hong_Kong) "IFC Mall (Hong Kong)"). In 2007, the company opened a store at [Pacific Place Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Place_(Hong_Kong) "Pacific Place (Hong Kong)"), Hong Kong, focusing on furniture and other lifestyle items. In July 2007, the company returned its presence in Beijing, with the opening of its store in Seasons Place Mall following a HK$300 million investment.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-8) The opening of the Beijing store follows the closing of other stores in Hangzhou, Shanghai, and Harbin following a strategy change.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-9)[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-10) During this time, Lane Crawford's focus shifted into becoming specialty department store selling speciality products like [haute couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haute_couture "Haute couture").[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-reuters2008-1)[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-11)

In 2012, its second Beijing store was opened at the [Yintai Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Yintai_Centre "Beijing Yintai Centre"). In October 2013, Lane Crawford opened its Shanghai flagship store at Shanghai Times Square.[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-12) In March 2014, the [Chengdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu") store was opened at Chengdu IFS.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-13) In 2014, after 21 years of service, the fashion director of Lane Crawford, Sarah Rutson, left the company.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-14)

In June 2017, Lane Crawford was subject to a significant number of complaints by Chinese consumers following mass cancellations of orders that have already been paid for. Following a meeting with the Consumer Protection Agency of China, the company issued a statement justifying the cancellations of 213 orders, citing erroneous pricing due to a systematic error on their website.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-15)

In 2020, the president of Lane Crawford, Andrew Keith, left the company after 9 years[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-16) and was replaced by Blondie Tsang.[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-17) Jennifer Woo is the current Chairman and CEO of the company.[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane_Crawford#cite_note-18)
